topic.topic: Hypothetical local inference speed: what the numbers do not show
topic.audience: r/LocalLLaMA readers running local language models
topic.scenario_status: Hypothetical experiment brief; not measured results or personal experience. State that status explicitly. Do not invent external facts or benchmarks.

facts.text: Two hypothetical runtimes achieve 18 and 24 tokens per second.
The hypothetical test uses one prompt on the same machine.
Time to first token and answer quality were not measured.
The sample does not establish a universal winner.

draft.title: Hypothetical Local LLM Inference: 18 vs 24 Tokens/Sec - What's Missing?
draft.body:
I've encountered some hypothetical performance figures for local LLM inference on a single machine, showing 18 tokens/sec and 24 tokens/sec for two different runtimes. While these numbers provide a basic comparison point, the brief explicitly states this is a hypothetical experiment and not measured results. Crucially, factors like time to first token and the actual quality of the generated answers were not part of this hypothetical test. This means we can't conclude which runtime is universally better, as speed alone doesn't tell the whole story. The provided figures (F1, F2) are limited to this specific setup and prompt.

This raises questions about how to interpret such synthetic benchmarks. What other metrics are critical for evaluating local inference performance beyond raw token generation speed, especially when factors like latency and output relevance are unknown? F3 and F4 highlight these limitations.
draft.plan: Discuss the limitations of the hypothetical benchmark, focusing on what metrics are missing beyond raw token speed. Invite discussion on the importance of time-to-first-token and answer quality in practical local LLM use cases, given the hypothetical nature of the provided data.

quality.reasons: The draft clearly states the hypothetical nature of the data and explicitly references the missing metrics (time to first token, answer quality). It avoids overclaiming and maintains a restrained tone. The title accurately reflects the content. The discussion invites critical thinking about interpreting synthetic benchmarks, which is highly relevant and useful for the target audience. The language is clear and technical, suitable for the intended readers.

draft.title: Interpreting Hypothetical LLM Speed: 18 & 24 Tokens/Sec on Same Hardware
draft.body:
A hypothetical scenario presents two local LLM inference runtimes achieving 18 and 24 tokens per second, respectively, when tested on the same machine with a single prompt (F1, F2). It's important to note that this remains a hypothetical experiment and does not represent measured results or personal experience. The brief explicitly states that critical metrics such as time to first token and the qualitative assessment of answer quality were not evaluated (F3). Therefore, these figures do not establish a definitive performance hierarchy or a universal winner between the two runtimes (F4).

This hypothetical data prompts a discussion on how to contextualize simple speed benchmarks. What are the implications of ignoring initial response latency and output fidelity in such comparisons? How can users best approach these kinds of synthetic performance figures, understanding their inherent constraints?
draft.plan: Frame the hypothetical token/sec figures as data points within a strictly defined, hypothetical test. Emphasize the unmeasured aspects (time to first token, answer quality) and the limited scope (single prompt, same machine). Pose questions about how to interpret such limited data and what additional information would be needed for a more comprehensive understanding of practical performance.

quality.reasons: This draft also faithfully preserves the hypothetical scenario and caveats, clearly stating the limitations of the data. The title matches the body content well. The text is well-structured and invites thoughtful discussion on interpreting limited synthetic benchmarks. It is clear, relevant, and credible, with no unsupported claims or exaggeration.
